questions_asked:
How many worker hornets does a single Vespa mandarinia nest typically raise
over one summer season?

When a giant-hornet nest is discovered, how quickly is it usually found and
destroyed by responders, and what typically triggers its discovery?

The problem says a new queen can travel about 30 km to found a nest. In the
real world, is 30 km a typical distance or an outer limit, and how far do most
queens actually fly?

From your experience, what makes a real giant-hornet sighting different from
people mistaking ordinary wasps or other hornets for one?

To confirm a report as a real giant hornet, does the state lab need a physical
specimen, or is a good photo sometimes enough?

During the busy summer reporting season, how often does the state review new
hornet reports to decide what to investigate next — daily, weekly, or as a
batch?

How long would it take without any confirmed giant-hornet sightings before you
would be reasonably confident the state was actually free of them?

Given limited staff, roughly how many hornet reports can the state realistically
investigate in a busy week during the peak summer season?

If you had to put one report at the very top of the list, what feature of it
would matter most — location, size, a bee-hive attack, or the time of year?

In the real world, if a giant hornet is genuinely present in an area, how often
does it actually get reported and confirmed — does almost every one turn up, or
are many missed?
expert_answers: A mature *Vespa mandarinia* colony typically produces on the order of a few hundred workers over the season — commonly cited as roughly 100–300 workers at peak, with some large nests reaching several hundred. This is an empirical estimate; exact counts vary widely with climate, prey availability, and nest age.

Discovery is usually triggered by a positive public or trapper report — a confirmed worker sighting, a live hornet caught in a trap, or a beekeeper reporting an attack on a hive — rather than by systematic searching. Once a detection is confirmed, responders typically locate and destroy the nest within days to a few weeks, since the nest must be physically found (often by tracking tagged hornets or following flight lines) before it can be removed. In practice, nests are often found late in the season, after workers are numerous and foraging widely, so the interval from first confirmed detection to nest eradication is commonly on the order of one to several weeks. This is an empirical judgment; timing varies with terrain, staffing, and how early the first credible report arrives.

30 km is an outer limit, not a typical distance. It is the maximum dispersal range attributed to a newly mated *Vespa mandarinia* queen; most queens found nests much closer to their natal nest — typically within a few kilometers, often under 1–2 km, when suitable habitat and nest sites are available. Long-distance dispersal on the order of 10–30 km is the tail of the distribution, occurring when queens are carried by wind or when local sites are saturated. So for modeling spread, treat 30 km as a rare maximum per-generation jump, not the expected dispersal distance. This is an empirical judgment; precise field measurements for this species are sparse.

The most reliable distinguishing features are size and the head/thorax coloration. *Vespa mandarinia* is conspicuously large — workers roughly 3–4 cm, queens up to ~5 cm, noticeably bigger than common yellowjackets, paper wasps, or European hornets. The key visual marker is the very large, bright orange-yellow head with prominent dark eyes, plus a mostly dark thorax and banded orange-and-dark abdomen. European hornets are similar in bulk but have a reddish-brown head and thorax, not the orange-yellow head.

In practice, most mistaken reports are ordinary wasps or yellowjackets, or the European hornet; people also misjudge scale from photos with no size reference. Genuine sightings usually come with a clear close-up showing the orange head, or a report of an unusually large hornet near honeybee hives. This is an empirical judgment based on how such reports are typically screened.

A good photo is often enough. State labs routinely confirm positive IDs from clear, close-up images showing the diagnostic features (large orange-yellow head, dark thorax, banded abdomen), especially when accompanied by a credible report. A physical specimen is preferred and is typically required when the image is ambiguous, lacks a size reference, or the record is otherwise borderline — but it is not mandatory for every confirmation. In practice, a substantial share of confirmed positives are photo-based, with specimens collected mainly for first-in-area detections or when genetic/authoritative verification is wanted. This is an empirical judgment about typical screening practice.

Daily, during the active season. In practice, state agriculture staff triage incoming reports essentially continuously — new reports are screened as they arrive, and follow-up decisions (trap checks, site visits, specimen requests) are made on a daily cadence, because a live hornet or a hive attack is time-sensitive. Batch review happens mainly in the off-season or when report volume is low, not during the summer peak. This is an empirical judgment about typical agency practice; exact cadence varies with staffing and volume.

There is no fixed clock that alone establishes freedom; it depends on surveillance intensity. Under continued active surveillance — traps plus public reporting — a reasonable working threshold is roughly **2–3 consecutive years with no confirmed detections** (including no trapped workers and no hive attacks), given the hornet's annual life cycle and the need to observe at least two full seasons of queen emergence and colony founding.

The logic: a single missed nest can release new queens each fall, so one quiet year is weak evidence. Two to three years of zero confirmed positives, with trapping and reporting maintained at normal effort, makes an undetected persisting population unlikely. If surveillance is reduced, the required period lengthens, because absence of detections then reflects absence of looking as much as absence of hornets.

This is an empirical judgment; the exact number depends on assumed detection probability and the acceptable residual-risk level.

Roughly a few dozen per week — on the order of 20–50 field investigations — is a realistic ceiling for a small state agriculture team during peak season. The binding constraint is staff time: a single site visit (travel, inspection, specimen handling, documentation) typically consumes a substantial fraction of a person-day, and only a handful of staff are assigned to hornet work. So with, say, 3–5 people devoting part of their week to field follow-up, the number of *investigations* is limited to tens, not hundreds.

Note the distinction: *screening* reports (desk review of photos and notes) can be done for hundreds per week, but *physical investigation* — trap checks, site visits, specimen collection — is the scarce resource at a few dozen per week. This is an empirical judgment; exact capacity scales with staffing and how far sites are from each other.

A bee-hive attack — a report of hornets attacking or destroying a honeybee hive — would matter most. It is the single strongest positive indicator because it is a behavioral signature that ordinary wasps and yellowjackets do not produce at that scale, and it implies multiple large hornets are present at a specific, actionable location. It also carries the highest urgency, since an active attack means a colony is being lost and a nest is likely nearby.

Location (inside a known detection zone) and time of year (late summer/fall, when colonies are large and workers forage widely) are useful secondary filters that raise prior probability, and reported size helps but is often misjudged. But a credible hive-attack report outranks all of these. This is an empirical judgment about screening practice.

Many are missed. Detection is strongly incomplete: a genuine hornet presence is usually only confirmed when a worker happens to be seen, trapped, or caught attacking a hive, and most hornets in an area never generate a confirmed report.

Real-world reasons: workers forage over wide areas and are inconspicuous individually; public reports are dominated by mistaken sightings, so genuine ones are diluted; traps sample only a small fraction of the landscape; and nests are hidden and often found late. So confirmed detections typically represent a small, biased subset of actual hornet activity — a "tip of the iceberg." Absence of confirmed reports is therefore weak evidence of absence unless surveillance effort is high and sustained.

This is an empirical judgment; the exact detection probability depends on trap density, reporting rates, and terrain.
